summary.title: Rosuvastatin at a glance
points: A statin: it slows cholesterol production in the liver. One tablet a day, any time, with or without food.
Three EU uses: high cholesterol from age 6, homozygous FH from age 6, and prevention of a first cardiovascular event in high-risk people.
LDL falls about 45–63% across 5–40 mg in a small dose study; the effect peaks by about four weeks.
The EU label describes JUPITER through post-hoc higher-risk analyses, not its overall result.
Watch muscles, liver tests, protein in urine at high doses, and a small diabetes signal.

exercises.scenario: A colleague says: 'Crestor is approved to prevent heart attacks in anyone with high cholesterol.'

questions.prompt: What does the Spanish SmPC actually cover for prevention?
options: Anyone who has already had a heart attack
High-risk people, before any first event
Anyone with LDL above their target
questions.explanation: The prevention indication is about a first event in high-risk people. There's no separate indication for people who have already had an event.

questions.prompt: Which kind of analysis does the EU label use to describe JUPITER?
options: A pooled analysis of all statin trials
The trial's overall primary result, as in the publication
questions.explanation: The EU SmPC gives two post-hoc analyses chosen after the data were seen. The US label gives the overall result.

exercises.scenario: A patient on rosuvastatin asks which blood tests matter.

questions.prompt: Which check does the SmPC ask for before starting and again at three months?
questions.explanation: Transaminases are checked before treatment and three months later. CK isn't checked routinely in people without symptoms.

questions.prompt: Why is the dose-table LDL figure (−52% at 10 mg) only 'orientation'?
options: It comes from the US label, not the EU SmPC
Tiny groups, and no stated duration
questions.explanation: Tiny groups make noisy numbers, and every number needs its time point.

summary.title: How it works
points: Blocks HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in the liver's cholesterol production.
The liver responds with more LDL receptors, which pull LDL out of the blood; it also makes less VLDL.
Only about 10% is metabolised; most leaves unchanged. Half-life about 19 hours.
Its interactions come mainly from transporters (OATP1B1, BCRP), not liver enzymes.
Asian patients have about twice the exposure: start at 5 mg, and 40 mg is contraindicated.

exercises.scenario: A pharmacist sees a patient on rosuvastatin who has just been prescribed ciclosporin after a transplant.

questions.prompt: What is the mechanism behind the problem?
questions.explanation: Rosuvastatin is barely metabolised. Its key interactions run through OATP1B1 and BCRP, and ciclosporin blocks them.

questions.prompt: What does the SmPC say about this combination?
questions.explanation: A 7-fold rise in exposure is too large to manage with a dose cap.

exercises.scenario: You're explaining to a partner why the label mentions ancestry and genes.

questions.prompt: A person known to carry the ABCG2 c.421AA variant needs rosuvastatin. What's the advice?
options: Half the usual dose, maximum 20 mg
Start at 40 mg because the transporter is weaker
questions.explanation: A weaker BCRP pump raises exposure about 2.4-fold, so the dose is halved and capped at 20 mg.

questions.prompt: Why does lowering liver cholesterol production lower LDL in the blood?
options: The liver adds more LDL receptors
The kidneys excrete more LDL in the urine
questions.explanation: Less cholesterol made inside the cell means more LDL receptors on its surface, so more LDL is pulled in.

summary.title: History
points: Discovered by Shionogi; developed by AstraZeneca as ZD4522. First EU approval: Netherlands, 2002.
The mutual recognition procedure was contested: Germany, Norway and Spain withdrew; France withdrew 40 mg.
An Article 29 referral (2005) settled the starting dose: 5 or 10 mg.
Approved first on LDL alone, a surrogate endpoint. Outcome trials came later, with mixed results.
Spain joined in 2008–2009 through a repeat-use procedure.

exercises.scenario: A business partner asks why Crestor launched in Spain six years after its first EU approval.

questions.prompt: What is the accurate explanation?
options: It withdrew in 2003, then joined by repeat use
It was approved centrally by the EMA in 2008
Spain required its own outcome trial before approving it
questions.explanation: Withdrawal isn't rejection. Spain came in through repeat use, with authorisations from November 2008 and January 2009.

questions.prompt: Which EU route settles disagreements between member states during mutual recognition?
options: A periodic safety update single assessment
questions.explanation: For Crestor it fixed the starting dose at 5 or 10 mg, made binding by the Commission in August 2005.

exercises.scenario: Think about what 'approved on LDL' meant for later decisions.

questions.prompt: Which trial result led to a new EU indication?
options: METEOR, leading to an indication to slow artery thickening
AURORA, leading to a dialysis indication
JUPITER, leading to the prevention indication in 2010
CORONA, leading to a heart-failure indication
questions.explanation: METEOR is described in the label but got no indication; CORONA and AURORA were neutral.

questions.prompt: Why were the Dutch assessors willing to keep 40 mg?
options: 40 mg had its own outcome trial data
The US had already approved 80 mg
40 mg was only used in children
questions.explanation: The answer to the safety debate was restriction: specialist start, severe cases, and several contraindications.

summary.title: What it's approved for
points: Every use is as an adjunct: diet and non-drug measures continue, and secondary causes are treated first.
High cholesterol (Fredrickson IIa and IIb, including heterozygous FH) from age 6; children only under specialists.
Homozygous FH from age 6: based on a 42-patient open-label study, no comparator.
Prevention of a first event in high-risk people, at 20 mg; 'high risk' is defined by JUPITER's post-hoc analyses.
Not in the EU label: raised triglycerides alone, plaque slowing (METEOR), heart failure (CORONA).

exercises.scenario: A marketing draft says: 'Crestor: approved for high triglycerides and to slow plaque build-up.'

questions.prompt: What's wrong with that claim for the Spanish label?
options: Only the plaque claim is wrong
Only the triglyceride claim is wrong
Nothing; both are approved in Spain
questions.explanation: Raised triglycerides alone appears in the US label, not the EU one. METEOR is only described in section 5.1.

questions.prompt: A patient's high cholesterol turns out to be caused by an underactive thyroid. What does the SmPC ask first?
questions.explanation: Secondary hypercholesterolaemia should be treated first.

exercises.scenario: Compare the EU and US labels.

questions.prompt: Where is the US label narrower than the EU one?
options: The US has no prevention indication
questions.explanation: The US door is wider elsewhere (triglycerides, dysbetalipoproteinaemia) but narrower on paediatric age.

questions.prompt: Why is the homozygous FH indication accepted on such thin evidence?
options: It was approved in the US first
It had a large placebo-controlled trial
It used LDL apheresis as comparator
questions.explanation: Rare diseases rarely allow large comparative trials.

summary.title: Strengths and products
points: Crestor in Spain: 5, 10 and 20 mg film-coated tablets, engraved ZD4522; lactose is the key excipient.
MAH in Spain: Grünenthal GmbH. Sold as Crestor in 17 EEA countries.
40 mg is on the Spanish market as generics referencing Crestor 40 mg, so the 40 mg rules still apply.
Generics (EFG) may be scored and split; some come in 15 and 30 mg, which Crestor never had.
Combinations with ezetimibe, fenofibrate, amlodipine, valsartan or aspirin are substitution therapy only.

exercises.scenario: A distributor asks whether they can launch a rosuvastatin/ezetimibe tablet as first-line treatment.

questions.prompt: What do the Spanish combination licences allow?
options: First-line, but only after a heart attack
questions.explanation: These fixed-dose combinations replace separate tablets; they aren't for starting treatment.

questions.prompt: A competitor sells rosuvastatin 15 mg. Why isn't it labelled as a generic?
options: Generics can't have a score line
Only the MAH may sell 15 mg
questions.explanation: A generic copies a reference product; a strength the reference never had can't be a generic of it.

exercises.scenario: The Spanish Crestor SmPC lists only 5, 10 and 20 mg.

questions.prompt: Why does it still contain 40 mg rules?
options: It's a printing error left over from the US label
The rules apply only in the US
40 mg generics exist; the EU text included it
questions.explanation: The label text comes from the common EU procedure, and the rules apply to every 40 mg tablet a patient might get.

questions.prompt: Which practical difference can matter for patients switching from Crestor to some generics?
options: Generics must be taken with food
questions.explanation: Small product differences, such as scoring, can be useful in practice.

summary.title: How it's taken
points: Once a day, any time, with or without food. Start at 5 or 10 mg; step up after 4 weeks.
Start at 5 mg if over 70, of Asian origin, with moderate kidney impairment, muscle risk factors, or interacting medicines.
Creatinine clearance below 30: contraindicated. Below 60: start at 5 mg, no 40 mg.
Liver tests before and at 3 months; stop or reduce if transaminases exceed 3× ULN.
CK isn't routine. Contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Missed dose: just take the next one.

exercises.scenario: A 74-year-old woman of Korean origin, normal kidneys, is starting Crestor for high cholesterol.

questions.prompt: What starting dose does the SmPC recommend?
options: 10 mg, with 40 mg available later if needed
5 mg, and 40 mg is contraindicated for her
questions.explanation: Both age over 70 and Asian origin point to 5 mg; Asian origin also rules out 40 mg.

questions.prompt: Her baseline CK comes back at 6× ULN. What next?
options: Repeat it; don't start if confirmed
Start at 5 mg anyway and recheck CK after exercise
questions.explanation: A baseline CK above 5× ULN is rechecked, and treatment isn't started if confirmed. Avoid testing after strenuous exercise.

exercises.scenario: A man with creatinine clearance of 45 mL/min isn't at goal on 20 mg.

questions.prompt: Can he go up to 40 mg?
options: No: 40 mg is barred below 60 mL/min
Yes, if a specialist starts it
Only if he takes it with food and a specialist agrees
questions.explanation: Moderate kidney impairment caps him below 40 mg. Other options (such as adding ezetimibe) come into play.

questions.prompt: He asks what to do if he forgets a dose.
options: Stop for a week and restart
Take two tablets the next day
Take the next one as usual; no doubling
questions.explanation: The PIL keeps it simple: no double dose.

summary.title: Reading a clinical trial
points: Check the primary endpoint and what a composite counts before comparing trials.
Give both absolute and relative risk reduction, with comparator and time.
HR below 1 with a CI that doesn't cross 1.0 is statistically significant.
NNT = 100 ÷ absolute risk reduction (percentage points), for a stated time.
Trials stopped early for benefit tend to overstate effects; prespecified beats post-hoc.

exercises.scenario: HOPE-3: 4.8% on placebo vs 3.7% on rosuvastatin over 5.6 years.

questions.prompt: What's the absolute risk reduction and NNT?
questions.explanation: 24% is the relative reduction. NNT uses the absolute difference: 100 ÷ 1.1 ≈ 91.

questions.prompt: HOPE-3's HR was 0.76 (95% CI 0.64–0.91). What does that mean?
questions.explanation: A CI entirely below 1.0 rules out 'no difference' at the usual level.

exercises.scenario: A slide claims JUPITER proves a 44% benefit, and CORONA 'showed an 8% benefit in heart failure'.

questions.prompt: What's wrong with the CORONA claim?
questions.explanation: p = 0.12. An HR of 0.92 with an interval crossing 1.0 isn't a demonstrated benefit.

questions.prompt: What caution applies to JUPITER's 44%?
options: It stopped early, which inflates effects
questions.explanation: Stopping at a moment when benefit looks large inflates the estimate; the true effect may be smaller.

summary.title: The pivotal trials
points: JUPITER: normal LDL, raised CRP; HR 0.56 for first events; stopped early at 1.9 years.
HOPE-3: intermediate risk, 10 mg fixed dose; 3.7% vs 4.8% over 5.6 years (HR 0.76).
METEOR: artery-wall thickening slowed; a surrogate, no indication.
CORONA (heart failure) and AURORA (dialysis): LDL fell, events didn't change.
The EU SmPC describes only JUPITER and METEOR.

exercises.scenario: A partner wants to promote rosuvastatin in dialysis clinics.

questions.prompt: What does the evidence and label say?
options: No benefit, and dialysis is contraindicated
The EU allows 5–10 mg in patients on dialysis
questions.explanation: AURORA: HR 0.96, not significant. The US allows 5–10 mg only in severe impairment not on dialysis.

questions.prompt: Which trial is described in the EU SmPC?
questions.explanation: Only JUPITER and METEOR appear in the EU SmPC.

exercises.scenario: Look at the pattern across the five trials.

questions.prompt: What does the pattern suggest?
options: Benefit without disease; none in HF or dialysis
It only lowers LDL, never events
It works equally well in every population studied
questions.explanation: JUPITER and HOPE-3 were positive; CORONA and AURORA neutral despite LDL falls.

questions.prompt: Why shouldn't you compare HOPE-3's LDL fall (−26.5%) with the SmPC dose table (−52% at 10 mg)?
options: The dose table is from the US
questions.explanation: Read each number in its own context.

summary.title: Combination trials
points: Fixed-dose combination: one tablet; co-administration: separate tablets taken together.
Licensed combinations in Spain are substitution only; many partners (telmisartan, SGLT2, PCSK9, bempedoic acid) have no EU combination licence.
SmPC lines: ezetimibe ×1.2, fibrates (no 40 mg), clopidogrel ×2, ticagrelor ×2.6.
RACING: rosuvastatin 10 + ezetimibe no worse than 20 mg over 3 years, with fewer treatment stops.
HOPE-3 combined arm (separate tablets): HR 0.71. Most BP combination trials are 8-week marker studies.

exercises.scenario: A licensing partner proposes a rosuvastatin + telmisartan single pill for the EU, citing 'outcome evidence'.

questions.prompt: What does the evidence actually support?
questions.explanation: HOPE-3 used candesartan with hydrochlorothiazide, as separate tablets. Telmisartan pairs only have short marker trials.

questions.prompt: What does the Crestor SmPC say about telmisartan?
questions.explanation: The SmPC has no line for aspirin, SGLT2 inhibitors, the BP medicines, PCSK9 inhibitors or bempedoic acid.

exercises.scenario: A cardiologist wonders whether to double the statin or add ezetimibe.

questions.prompt: What did RACING show?
options: Ezetimibe was clearly superior on cardiovascular deaths
It compared against a PCSK9 inhibitor
10 mg + ezetimibe was no worse than 20 mg
questions.explanation: Non-inferiority, within a 2-point margin: about 9.0% vs 9.9% at 3 years.

questions.prompt: What limits applying RACING's doses directly to European patients?
options: It excluded people with heart disease
questions.explanation: Ancestry affects exposure (Lesson 2); it was also open-label.

summary.title: Heart-attack and stroke outcomes
points: JUPITER: heart attacks HR 0.46, strokes HR 0.52, over a median of 1.9 years; effects may be overstated.
Death: HR 0.80 across JUPITER, but not significant in the EU label's post-hoc slices.
No effect on death in heart failure (CORONA, GISSI-HF) or dialysis (AURORA).
LODESTAR vs atorvastatin: similar hard outcomes (HR 1.06), more new diabetes and cataract surgery.
CTT: per 1 mmol/L lower LDL, about 22% fewer major vascular events and 10% fewer deaths (class, relative).

exercises.scenario: Two documents disagree: the JUPITER paper says deaths fell; the EU SmPC says they didn't.

questions.prompt: Which is right?
options: Both: different slices of one trial
questions.explanation: Whole trial HR 0.80; the two post-hoc analyses weren't significant for death (p = 0.193 and 0.076).

questions.prompt: What does LODESTAR add that placebo trials can't?
questions.explanation: Only LODESTAR compares two active statins directly.

exercises.scenario: A payer asks how big the benefit is for a low-risk 50-year-old.

questions.prompt: How should you use the CTT figure (22% fewer events per 1 mmol/L)?
options: It's relative; absolute depends on risk
Use 22% as the absolute reduction for any patient
questions.explanation: Low baseline risk means a small absolute gain, even with the same relative effect.

questions.prompt: Why read the three outcome columns (placebo, head-to-head, advanced disease) separately?
options: They all used the 40 mg dose
questions.explanation: Cross-trial comparisons mislead.

summary.title: Side effects
points: Common: headache, dizziness, gut upset, muscle aches, weakness, diabetes (depends on risk factors).
Rare but serious: rhabdomyolysis (more above 20 mg), DRESS and SJS (never restart), immune-mediated necrotising myopathy, myasthenia.
Protein in urine: about 3% at 40 mg, usually transient, not shown to predict kidney disease.
Diabetes: more in JUPITER and LODESTAR, not HOPE-3. The SmPC says monitor, don't stop.
Cataract: seen in LODESTAR and HOPE-3, absent from the label.

exercises.scenario: A patient with fasting glucose of 6.1 mmol/L and BMI 32 is starting rosuvastatin.

questions.prompt: What does the SmPC say about her diabetes risk?
questions.explanation: Risk factors raise the chance of diabetes, but that isn't a reason to withhold the statin.

questions.prompt: Months later she develops a widespread rash, fever and swollen glands. What's the rule?
options: Pause for a week, then restart
questions.explanation: DRESS and Stevens-Johnson syndrome are permanent contraindications to rechallenge.

exercises.scenario: Your team is drafting a safety summary for a partner.

questions.prompt: Which signal appears in trials but not in the Crestor SmPC?
questions.explanation: A trial finding the label hasn't taken up. Not proof of harm, but worth tracking.

questions.prompt: Muscle weakness and raised CK persist after stopping the statin. What should you suspect?
options: An exercise-related CK rise that will settle with rest
questions.explanation: Unlike ordinary statin myopathy, it doesn't settle when the statin is stopped.

summary.title: Who shouldn't take it, and interactions
points: Never: active liver disease, CrCl below 30, myopathy, ciclosporin, sofosbuvir/velpatasvir/voxilaprevir, pregnancy or breastfeeding.
No 40 mg: CrCl below 60, hypothyroidism, muscle history, alcohol abuse, Asian origin, fibrates, higher-exposure situations.
2× rule: if a co-medicine doubles exposure or more, start at 5 mg and cap so exposure stays ≤ 40 mg alone.
Fusidic acid: stop rosuvastatin during treatment and for 7 days after.
Antacids halve levels (take 2 hours later); monitor INR with vitamin K antagonists.

exercises.scenario: A patient on rosuvastatin 20 mg is starting gemfibrozil (×1.9 exposure).

questions.prompt: What does the 2× rule imply?
options: Go up to 40 mg to overcome the interaction
questions.explanation: The cap keeps exposure at or below 40 mg alone. Gemfibrozil is also 'not recommended' with rosuvastatin.

questions.prompt: The same patient needs systemic fusidic acid for an infection.
options: Continue at 5 mg and check CK weekly
questions.explanation: Rhabdomyolysis, including deaths, has been reported with the combination.

exercises.scenario: An EU–US label comparison is going into a partner deck.

questions.prompt: How does the US label handle cyclosporine?
questions.explanation: The US label's contraindications are limited to acute liver failure, decompensated cirrhosis and hypersensitivity.

questions.prompt: The PIL warns about severe respiratory insufficiency, but the SmPC doesn't. What's the right reaction?
options: Flag it for the next review
questions.explanation: PILs should reflect the SmPC; a PIL-only line is worth flagging.

summary.title: Pharmacovigilance
points: PSURs are assessed together across companies in a PSUSA; rosuvastatin's (data to Nov 2022) ended in maintenance.
The ezetimibe/rosuvastatin PSUSA (data to July 2020) added DRESS and the ticagrelor interaction to every rosuvastatin label.
PRAC 2023: all statins warn about myasthenia gravis.
Early safety decisions still stand: no 80 mg, restricted 40 mg, lower Asian starting dose.
Watchlist: cataract, and the PIL-only respiratory line.

exercises.scenario: Your company holds a rosuvastatin + amlodipine licence, not an ezetimibe one.

questions.prompt: Did the DRESS conclusion from the ezetimibe/rosuvastatin review affect your label?
options: Yes: it applied to all rosuvastatin products
No, it applied only to ezetimibe combination products
questions.explanation: A signal found through one combination can change all labels containing the substance.

questions.prompt: What does 'maintenance' as a PSUSA outcome mean?
questions.explanation: Maintenance means the benefit-risk balance and the label stay as they are.

exercises.scenario: You're planning the module refresh calendar.

questions.prompt: Which event should trigger an immediate refresh?
options: A new generic rosuvastatin launch in Spain
A combination PSUSA ending in a variation
questions.explanation: Also: a new SmPC revision, or a PRAC signal on statins or rosuvastatin.

questions.prompt: Why is cataract on the watchlist rather than in the label?
options: It's in the US label only
It only occurs at the withdrawn 80 mg dose
A trial signal not yet assessed by PRAC
questions.explanation: A trial signal isn't proof of harm; regular review is designed to catch such items.

summary.title: ESC guidelines
points: Guidelines advise; they don't change licences. Classes I–III, evidence levels A–C.
2019: high-intensity statin to the highest tolerated dose (I A), then ezetimibe (I B), then PCSK9 inhibitor (I A).
Rosuvastatin 20 mg is high intensity, 10 mg moderate; the label still restricts 40 mg.
2025: after ACS, statin plus ezetimibe can start together in hospital (IIa B); bempedoic acid for intolerance (I B).
Combination tablets are substitution only: start separate tablets, switch once doses are settled.

exercises.scenario: After an acute coronary syndrome, a doctor wants to start rosuvastatin + ezetimibe together, as the 2025 update suggests.

questions.prompt: How do you do that within the Spanish licences?
options: Start the combination tablet straight away
questions.explanation: The guideline and the label work at different levels; the combination tablets are licensed for substitution.

questions.prompt: What does a 'IIa B' recommendation mean?
questions.explanation: Class IIa = should be considered; level B = one randomised trial or large non-randomised studies.

exercises.scenario: The guideline says 'highest tolerated dose'; the label restricts 40 mg.

questions.prompt: Which sets the outer limit?
questions.explanation: Guidance has to work inside the licence's limits.

questions.prompt: A very-high-risk patient after a heart attack isn't at goal on a high-intensity statin plus ezetimibe. What's the next 2019 step?
options: Add fenofibrate to lower triglycerides further
questions.explanation: Statin → ezetimibe → PCSK9 inhibitor in very-high-risk secondary prevention.

summary.title: The medicine and its story
points: A liver-targeted statin: blocks HMG-CoA reductase, more LDL receptors, LDL falls about half.
Interactions come from transporters (OATP1B1, BCRP), which explains ciclosporin and ancestry effects.
A contested EU start: withdrawals in 2003, an Article 29 referral on the starting dose, 40 mg restricted.
Approved on LDL; JUPITER later brought the prevention indication, other trials didn't.

exercises.scenario: A new BD colleague asks you to explain rosuvastatin's 'personality' in a partner meeting.

questions.prompt: Which link between mechanism and label is correct?
options: Its fungal origin explains muscle effects
Its short half-life explains once-daily dosing
questions.explanation: Rosuvastatin is barely metabolised; OATP1B1 and BCRP drive exposure.

questions.prompt: Why did the 2005 Article 29 referral matter for today's label?
options: It fixed the 5 or 10 mg starting dose
It moved Crestor to the centralised procedure
questions.explanation: The CHMP accepted either starting dose, chosen by cholesterol level and risk.

exercises.scenario: Connect history with safety.

questions.prompt: How do today's 40 mg restrictions trace back to the early years?
options: Early concerns led to restriction, not removal
They came from the 2023 PRAC signal on statins
questions.explanation: 80 mg was dropped; 40 mg kept with specialist start, severe cases, and contraindications.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the evidence base at first approval is true?
options: CORONA's outcome data supported the first approval
No outcome data; LDL as a surrogate
questions.explanation: Outcome trials came later.

questions.prompt: Why does the EU label start at 5 mg for Asian patients?
questions.explanation: Higher exposure means more risk; 40 mg is also contraindicated.

summary.title: The label in practice
points: Three EU uses, all as an adjunct; prevention is for a first event, defined by JUPITER's post-hoc analyses.
Products: Crestor 5–20 mg, generics up to 40 mg (some 15 and 30 mg), substitution-only combinations.
Dosing: start 5 or 10 mg; 5 mg for over-70s, Asian origin, CrCl below 60, interactions.
40 mg: severe cases at high risk, not at goal on 20 mg, under a specialist.

exercises.scenario: A 68-year-old white man with CrCl 75 mL/min, heterozygous FH, LDL still high on 20 mg after 4 weeks.

questions.prompt: What does the label allow next?
options: Not possible; 20 mg is the maximum
Switch to a combination tablet now
questions.explanation: He has no 40 mg contraindication (under 70, not Asian, CrCl ≥ 60, no fibrate).

questions.prompt: He'd like ezetimibe added in one tablet straight away. What fits the Spanish licences?
options: Ezetimibe can't be combined with 40 mg
Combination tablets don't exist in Spain
questions.explanation: Combinations are substitution therapy only.

exercises.scenario: A partner's dossier lists 'raised triglycerides' and '15 mg Crestor-equivalent generic' in its plan.

questions.prompt: What's wrong with the triglyceride indication for the EU?
options: It's only for the 40 mg dose
It needs a paediatric study first
questions.explanation: It exists in the US label, not the EU one.

questions.prompt: What's wrong with calling a 15 mg tablet a 'generic'?
options: 15 mg is only authorised for children
questions.explanation: It's authorised, just not as a generic.

questions.prompt: Who must start at 5 mg?
options: A 55-year-old with normal kidneys and no risk factors
questions.explanation: Over 70 is one of the 5 mg starting groups. Switching from a higher dose of another statin still starts at 5 or 10 mg.

summary.title: The evidence
points: Read every result with comparator, time, absolute and relative effect; check CI against 1.0.
Positive in people without established disease (JUPITER, HOPE-3); neutral in heart failure and dialysis.
Combinations: RACING (ezetimibe) and HOPE-3's combined arm are the only outcome evidence; the rest are 8-week marker trials.
Head-to-head vs atorvastatin (LODESTAR): similar outcomes, more diabetes and cataract.

exercises.scenario: A competitor's slide: 'Rosuvastatin cuts events by 44% (JUPITER) and is superior to atorvastatin.'

questions.prompt: What's the best correction for the first claim?
options: It's relative, from a trial stopped early
44% is the absolute reduction in heart attacks
questions.explanation: Always pair relative with absolute and note early stopping.

questions.prompt: And the second claim?
questions.explanation: Same outcomes; more new diabetes and cataract surgery on rosuvastatin.

exercises.scenario: A partner wants to position a rosuvastatin + candesartan + HCTZ polypill using HOPE-3.

questions.prompt: What's the key limitation?
options: HOPE-3 was negative for the combined arm
questions.explanation: HR 0.71 over 5.6 years, but as co-administration, not a single pill.

questions.prompt: Which trials suggest LDL lowering isn't enough in advanced disease?
questions.explanation: LDL fell by over 40% in both, but events didn't change.

questions.prompt: RACING's result was −0.78 points (95% CI −2.39 to 0.83) with a 2.0-point margin. What does it show?
options: Nothing, since the CI crosses zero
questions.explanation: For non-inferiority, the question is whether the interval stays within the margin, not whether it crosses zero.

summary.title: Safety and guidelines
points: Muscle risk rises with dose and exposure; most interactions raise exposure via transporters.
Never restart after DRESS or SJS; stop for fusidic acid; contraindicated with ciclosporin.
EU safety reviews (PSUSA, PRAC) added DRESS, ticagrelor and myasthenia to every label.
Guidelines push intensity and early ezetimibe; the label sets the limits.

exercises.scenario: A 66-year-old after ACS is on rosuvastatin 20 mg and is starting ticagrelor.

questions.prompt: What does the label point to?
options: Stop rosuvastatin permanently and switch class
A 2.6× rise: lower and cap the dose
questions.explanation: It entered the label through the ezetimibe/rosuvastatin PSUSA. The 2× rule applies.

questions.prompt: He's also at diabetes risk. What does the SmPC advise?
questions.explanation: Diabetes risk isn't a reason to stop.

exercises.scenario: Your partner asks how safety knowledge reaches the label, and what guidelines can change.

questions.prompt: Which route added the myasthenia warning?
options: A PRAC class signal on statins
questions.explanation: Class signals apply to every statin and combination containing one.

questions.prompt: Can the ESC 2025 update make the rosuvastatin/ezetimibe tablet a first-line product?
options: Yes, once the update is six months old
questions.explanation: Follow the guideline with separate tablets, then switch.

questions.prompt: In your own words: why is cataract on the watchlist, and what would have to happen for it to enter the label?
questions.modelAnswer: Two trials (LODESTAR, HOPE-3) showed more cataract surgery on rosuvastatin, but no regulatory assessment has confirmed a causal signal. It would enter through a PRAC signal assessment or a PSUSA ending with a variation.

summary.title: Rosuvastatin: the whole picture
points: A transporter-sensitive statin: exposure, not metabolism, drives its dosing rules and interactions.
Three EU uses; prevention is for a first event, framed by JUPITER's post-hoc analyses.
Evidence: positive without established disease, neutral in heart failure and dialysis, equal to atorvastatin.
Combinations: substitution only; outcome evidence mainly from RACING and HOPE-3.
Safety: muscle, diabetes and cataract signals; DRESS and myasthenia came from EU reviews.
Guidelines push intensity; the label sets the limits.

exercises.scenario: You're assessing a licensing opportunity: a rosuvastatin/ezetimibe FDC for Spain, marketed to cardiologists after ACS.

questions.prompt: Which claim would be acceptable in promotion?
options: For patients stable on both separately
Proven to cut deaths vs 20 mg alone
questions.explanation: The licence is substitution-only; RACING showed non-inferiority on events, not fewer deaths.

questions.prompt: Which evidence best supports the pairing?
questions.explanation: RACING is the combination outcome trial; note Korean exposure differences.

questions.prompt: Which safety line from the EU label must be in the training for reps?
options: Cataract as a labelled side effect
questions.explanation: DRESS reached every rosuvastatin label via the ezetimibe/rosuvastatin PSUSA. Cataract isn't labelled.

exercises.scenario: A patient story ties the module together: 72, of Chinese origin, CrCl 55, after a first heart attack, starting ticagrelor.

questions.prompt: What's the right starting dose?
questions.explanation: Over 70, Asian origin, CrCl below 60 and a ×2.6 interaction all point to 5 mg.

questions.prompt: Could she ever take 40 mg?
questions.explanation: Two separate 40 mg contraindications.

questions.prompt: If she isn't at goal, what does the guideline path suggest within the label's limits?
options: Increase to 40 mg under specialist supervision
Add ezetimibe, then a PCSK9 inhibitor
questions.explanation: Intensify by adding agents when the statin dose is capped.
